newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chef Ducasse falls star short of Michelin jackpot.
newsitem.headline: Chef Ducasse falls star short of Michelin jackpot.

text.p: Chef Alain Ducasee fell a star short of the Michelin jackpot on Monday as France's best known restaurant guide awarded his new Paris eatery three stars but took a third star away from his glitzy Louis XV in Monte Carlo.

The 1997 Michelin guide, released on Monday, rewarded the Frenchman who had hoped to become Michelin's first six-star chef with its highest rating for his Restaurant Alain Ducasse in the posh Parc Victor Hugo Hotel in Paris' 16th district.
But the guidebook, which is to France's great chefs what the Oscars are to the Hollywood film industry, demoted the Monte Carlo restaurant to two-star rank.
Ducasse, who is 40, has run the Louis XV kitchen since its opening in the lobby of the swank Hotel de Paris near the Monte Carlo casinos. It had enjoyed three-star status for the past seven years.
He took over the Paris restaurant in August from Joel Robuchon, thought by many to be France's greatest chef. Robuchon retired last year at 51 after 36 years in the kitchen.

Critics speculated the move was Michelin director-general Bernard Naegellen's way of sending a message that a chef must operate full-time in the kitchen to earn the bright red guide's supreme blessing.
Ducasse believes in leaving the day-to-day operations of his kitchens to his staff but nonetheless flies often between Paris and Monte Carlo to keep both establishments running smoothly.
The Paris restaurant offers classic French cuisine while the Louis XV specialises in Mediterranean cooking, with both charging astronomical prices.

The number of three-star restaurants in France stood at 18 in the new guide, with the list unchanged from the previous year's guide apart from Robuchon's retirement and Ducasse's simultaneous rise and fall.
Five of the top-ranked establishments are in Paris.
But reinforcing a trend, the staid Michelin awarded at least one of its coveted stars to just 515 restaurants this year, down from 532 last year, 541 in 1995 and 554 for 1994.

Similarly, Michelin rival Gault-Millau, whose 1997 guide came out in November, gave its highest rating of four "toques" -- the traditional towering white chef's cap -- to just 12 restaurants this year, down sharply from a few years ago.
The development has triggered speculation that the quality of France's top restaurants is gradually declining.
But Michelin officials blame the drop on bad economic times.

With French unemployment at just under 13 percent and tight family budgets around the world, it is no wonder that fewer people are going to restaurants where a dinner can easily cost over a thousand francs (hundreds of dollars) a person, they say.

In another closely watched move, the new Michelin awarded a respectable two stars to the new Paris eatery opened this year by Pierrre Gagnaire, whose previous restaurant in the depressed central town of Saint Etienne last year became the first three-star in Michelin history to go bankrupt.
Gagnaire's new restaurant in the Hotel Balzac in Paris'S Latin Quarter seats just 40. A fixed-price dinner without wine is a relatively reasonable 350 francs ($60).
